KEY MESSAGE 1...

Surface low pressure will continue tracking eastward toward the
Mid-Atlantic coast this afternoon as a secondary polar cold
front pushes southeastward through western Pennsylvania, eastern
Ohio, and northern West Virginia. Behind the front, surface
observations across the upper Ohio Valley indicate winds 
shifting west-northwest to northwest at 10 to 15 mph with gusts 
near 20 mph, accompanied by widespread low stratus and patchy 
light rain or drizzle. Temperatures will hold steady or slowly 
fall through the 40s this afternoon before dropping into the mid
to upper 30s across the lower elevations tonight, and into the 
lower 30s across the Laurel Highlands and the higher ridges of 
Preston and Tucker counties. With freezing levels lowering from
around 5200 ft on the 12Z PIT sounding to roughly 3000 to 4000 
ft by early Friday morning, lingering light rain showers will 
begin mixing with and changing to wet snow across the highest 
elevations before daybreak Friday, while lower elevations remain
all rain tonight. 

By Friday morning, expansive surface high pressure will settle
across the Missouri Valley, Lake Superior, and Michigan,
establishing a persistent corridor of cold northerly to north-
northwesterly flow at 320 to 350 degrees and 15 to 25KT through
the H925 to H850 layer across the warm waters of Lake Huron and
Lake Erie through early Sunday morning. With H850 temperatures 
cooling to -4C to -7C over lake surface temperatures in the 
upper single digits to low teens C, lake-induced instability 
will generate isolated to scattered lake-enhanced moisture 
streamers extending southward into western Pennsylvania, eastern
Ohio, and northern West Virginia. These streamers will be most 
common during the daytime hours on Friday and Saturday, when 
modest boundary-layer heating steepens low-level lapse rates and
promotes shallow cellular convection. Across the lower 
elevations, daytime highs will reach the upper 30s to lower 40s,
but surface dew points falling to near the freezing mark at 30 
to 33F. Any more intense daytime streamer will be capable of 
evaporatively cooling the near-surface layer to near 32 to 34F, 
allowing wet snowflakes to mix in and produce localized 
visibility reductions below 2 miles. However, limited band 
intensity, warm antecedent ground temperatures, and the still
quite high mid-November sun angle will limit snow accumulation 
across the lowlands. 

Across the higher terrain, subfreezing temperatures from early 
Friday morning through Sunday morning will support snow as the 
primary precipitation type. Forecast soundings show moisture 
remaining relatively shallow beneath a lowering subsidence 
inversion near H800 to H750 between 6500 and 8500 ft, where 
cloud-top temperatures of -6C to -12C only marginally reach the
dendritic growth zone of -12C to -18C. Furthermore, the 
predominantly northerly boundary-layer flow is less orthogonal 
to the southwest-to-northeast oriented Allegheny ridges than a 
typical west-northwest upslope event, limiting orographic lift 
and preventing streamers from remaining anchored over a single 
ridge. With total liquid-equivalent precipitation generally 
under 0.10 to 0.25 inches, most mountain locations will see 
less than an inch of snow, with localized accumulations of 1 to 
2 inches possible only where bands maintain cohesiveness along 
favored north facing slopes. Any lingering flurries or isolated 
snow showers will diminish by early Sunday morning as the 
upstream high shifts east and cuts off the Great Lakes moisture 
fetch. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Beyond Sunday morning, the expansive surface high pressure
system will build directly over the Ohio Valley and central
Appalachians while mid and upper-level ridging amplifies across
the eastern United States. Increasing subsidence and low-level 
winds backing to light northeasterly and easterly will scour out
residual Great Lakes stratocumulus by Sunday afternoon, 
ushering in a prolonged period of dry and quiet weather through 
at least Thursday. 

Daytime highs will remain chilly in the upper 30s to mid 40s on
Sunday, then gradually moderate through the upper 40s and lower
50s on Monday and Tuesday before reaching the mid to upper 50s 
by Wednesday and Thursday as warm air advection develops on the 
western periphery of the departing ridge.
